summary: Find the answer that makes the conclusion more likely to be true.
ideas: Identify the conclusion and the premises; the gap between them is the assumption.
A strengthener supports the assumption, rules out an alternative explanation, or adds evidence for the conclusion.
It does not need to prove the conclusion, only to make it more likely.
method: Find the conclusion (look for “therefore”, “so”, “thus”, or the claim the rest supports).
Predict the gap: what must be true for the premises to lead to the conclusion?
Choose the answer that closes the gap or removes an alternative.
traps: Answers that repeat a premise without helping the link.
Out of scope: a different group, time or place.
Answers that weaken instead.
shortcuts: For a causal conclusion (X causes Y), “no other cause” or “when X is absent, Y is absent” strengthens.

summary: Find the answer that most damages the link from premises to conclusion.
ideas: Premises are taken as true: attack the reasoning, not the facts.
Classic weakeners: an alternative cause, a sample that is not representative, a plan that will not reach its goal, an assumption that fails.
method: Find the conclusion and the premises.
Predict the assumption, then look for an answer that breaks it.
For causal arguments, look for another cause of the same effect, or for reversed causation.
traps: Answers that attack a premise rather than the reasoning.
Answers that are irrelevant to the specific conclusion.
Answers that actually strengthen.
shortcuts: Causal conclusion? Ask: what else could explain the result?

example.q: A company introduced flexible working hours, and the next year sick days fell by 15%. Management concluded that flexible hours reduced sick days. What would weaken this?
example.a: An alternative cause of the same effect, for example that the flu season that year was far milder than the year before.

summary: Find the unstated premise the argument needs.
ideas: A necessary assumption must be true for the argument to work.
Negation test: negate the answer; if the argument falls apart, it is the assumption.
Assumptions often link a new term in the conclusion to the premises.
method: Find the conclusion and premises.
Look for the new idea in the conclusion that the premises never mention.
Negate each remaining answer and keep the one that destroys the argument.
traps: Extreme answers (“all”, “always”, “never”) are rarely necessary.
Answers that would help but are not required.
shortcuts: Weak, modest wording (“at least some”, “not all”) fits necessary assumptions.

summary: Find the question or information that would best judge the argument.
ideas: The right answer is a question whose answer can strengthen or weaken the argument.
Variance test: imagine two opposite answers; one should help the argument and the other should hurt it.
method: Find the conclusion and the gap.
For each answer, imagine “yes” and “no”.
Keep the one where the two answers move the conclusion in opposite directions.
traps: Questions whose answer would not affect the conclusion either way.
Questions about details outside the argument.

summary: Find what must be true, or is best supported, given the statements.
ideas: There is often no conclusion: you draw one yourself.
The answer must follow from the text, with no outside knowledge.
Correct answers are usually cautiously worded.
method: Read the statements as facts.
Combine two of them to see what follows.
Eliminate anything that needs an extra assumption.
traps: Extreme words (“most”, “always”, “only”) that the text does not support.
Answers that sound reasonable but are not stated or implied.
Answers that use real-world knowledge.

summary: Describe the role each bold part plays in the argument.
ideas: Roles: main conclusion, intermediate conclusion, premise (evidence), opposing view, evidence against the conclusion, background.
The answer choices describe roles abstractly: match function, not content.
method: Find the author’s main conclusion first.
Label each bold part in your own words (conclusion, evidence for it, opposing claim, …).
Match your labels to the answers; eliminate any answer with one wrong label.
traps: Confusing the author’s conclusion with a position the author rejects.
Missing contrast words (“however”, “but”) that change who is speaking.
shortcuts: Contrast words usually introduce the author’s own view.

summary: Name the error in the reasoning.
ideas: Common flaws: correlation taken as causation, a sample that is not representative, circular reasoning, confusing percentages with numbers, false choice between two options, generalising from one case.
Answers describe the flaw in general terms.
method: Find the conclusion and the evidence.
Predict the gap in your own words.
Match it to the abstract description in the answers.
traps: Answers describing a flaw the argument does not commit.
Criticisms that are true but not the main problem.

summary: Resolve two facts that seem to contradict each other.
ideas: Both facts are true; the right answer shows how they can both be true.
The answer usually adds information about a difference between the two situations.
method: State the two facts and why they seem to conflict.
Look for the answer that makes the surprise go away.
traps: Answers that explain only one of the two facts.
Answers that make the conflict worse.

summary: Judge whether a plan reaches its goal, or describe how an argument works.
ideas: Plan questions: a goal and a plan to reach it; ask what makes the plan more or less likely to work.
Method questions: describe the technique of the argument (analogy, counterexample, questioning evidence, pointing to an alternative).
method: Separate the goal from the plan.
Look for side effects or conditions that would stop the plan from working.
For method questions, describe what the argument does in general words before reading the answers.
traps: Answers about a different goal.
Method answers that are accurate for part of the argument but not its main move.

summary: Primary purpose or main point of a passage.
ideas: The main idea covers the whole passage, not one paragraph.
The verb in the answer matters: argue, describe, explain, criticise, compare, propose.
method: After reading, state the main point in one sentence before looking at the answers.
Check the verb and the scope of each answer against the whole passage.
traps: Answers that are too narrow (one paragraph) or too broad (beyond the passage).
A wrong verb: “argue” when the passage only describes.
shortcuts: The first and last paragraphs usually carry the main point.

ideas: The answer is in the text, usually paraphrased.
Line references or key words tell you where to look.
method: Go back to the relevant sentence and reread it.
Match the meaning, not the same words.
traps: Answers that use the passage’s words with a changed meaning.
Statements that are true in the real world but not in the passage.
Details from the wrong paragraph.

summary: What the passage suggests or implies.
ideas: The answer goes one small step beyond the text, never far.
It must be supported by specific sentences.
method: Find the relevant sentences.
Ask what must be true if they are true.
Eliminate extreme and unsupported answers.
traps: Answers that go too far or need outside knowledge.
Extreme wording.

summary: Why the author mentions something, or how the passage is organised.
ideas: The question asks for purpose, not content.
Look at the sentences before and after the reference.
method: Find the reference in the passage.
Ask: what does this help the author do here?
Choose the answer that names that role.
traps: Answers that describe what the text says instead of why it is there.
shortcuts: Structure answers list the moves of the passage in order; check each move.

summary: Apply the passage’s idea or principle to a new situation.
ideas: The new situation has the same logical structure as the one in the passage.
method: State the principle in general terms.
Find the answer whose situation follows the same structure.
traps: Answers with the same topic but a different logic.

ideas: GMAT authors are usually moderate: qualified approval, measured scepticism, cautious optimism.
Adjectives and hedging words reveal the tone.
method: Collect the words that show the author’s opinion.
Choose the answer with the same strength and direction.
traps: Extreme emotions (outrage, contempt) are almost never right.
Confusing the author’s tone with the tone of views the author reports.
